paragraphs: A model’s average accuracy does not establish whether its answer to a particular question is correct. This paper proposes Self-Proving models, which produce an answer and then participate in an interactive proof with a verification algorithm. The aim is to make correctness something the verifier can check for the input at hand.

The framework separates two guarantees. On inputs drawn from a specified distribution, a Self-Proving model should, with high probability, both answer correctly and successfully prove its answer. Separately, the verifier’s soundness property prevents any model from persuading it to accept an incorrect answer on any input. Successful answering and proving is therefore a distribution-level property, while rejection of incorrect answers comes from the verifier.

The authors develop and analyze two generic training methods. Transcript Learning uses records of interactions that the verifier accepted. Reinforcement Learning from Verifier Feedback instead trains through simulated interactions with the verifier. These methods provide theoretical routes toward models whose accepted answers carry verification, rather than relying solely on aggregate accuracy.
neurips-2025-a-theory-for-worst-case-vs-.tldr: Self-Proving models combine learned answers with interactive verification, separating average success at proving answers from sound rejection of incorrect ones.

paragraphs: Scientific measurement often requires combining information across many individual items. AI can predict these measurements at scale, but predictions alone may not supply the accuracy or statistical guarantees researchers need. Active measurement combines model predictions with selectively collected human labels to estimate an overall total.

The process is iterative. An AI model predicts measurements for individual units, and importance sampling selects units for human labeling. Each new batch of labels serves two purposes: it improves the model and refines an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of the total. The authors develop estimators, weighting schemes, and confidence intervals to support this combined learning and measurement process.

The central benefit is that precise aggregate measurement can remain possible even when the model is imperfect. When the model is very accurate, the framework can require little human effort. Across several measurement tasks, the authors report lower estimation error than alternatives. The result supports using AI to guide human measurement effort while retaining a statistically grounded estimate of the quantity researchers actually want.
neurips-2025-active-measurement-efficien.tldr: Active measurement combines AI predictions with selectively sampled human labels to refine unbiased totals and reduce measurement error.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow models generate strong images but often require many sampling steps. Consistency models compress generation into one step, yet the authors show analytically and empirically that their performance degrades as the number of steps increases. This motivates flow maps, which connect any two noise levels in one step and remain effective across step counts.

Align Your Flow introduces two continuous-time objectives for learning these maps, together with additional training techniques. The objectives generalize existing consistency and flow-matching objectives. The authors also use autoguidance, where a lower-quality model supplies guidance during distillation. Adversarial fine-tuning provides another improvement, with a reported minimal reduction in sample diversity.

On ImageNet at 64-by-64 and 512-by-512 resolution, the resulting models achieve state-of-the-art few-step generation performance using small, efficient networks. The text-to-image models also outperform existing few-step samplers that were trained without adversarial methods. These findings support flow maps as a way to make compressed generators effective under different sampling budgets, instead of optimizing only for a single generation step.
neurips-2025-align-your-flow-scaling-con.tldr: Align Your Flow trains continuous-time flow maps for strong few-step image generation across different sampling step counts.

paragraphs: Text can involve AI in several ways: a person may edit an AI draft, an AI may revise human writing, or one AI may refine another’s output. These processes produce different but related textual characteristics. DETree addresses the difficulty of detecting such mixtures, including cases involving unfamiliar language models.

The authors observe clustering relationships among representations of texts produced through different processes. They organize those relationships into a Hierarchical Affinity Tree and introduce a loss function that trains text representations to follow its structure. This gives the detector a richer description of collaboration than either a human-versus-AI label or a single additional category for mixed authorship.

To support this training, the authors build RealBench, a benchmark that automatically incorporates a broad range of hybrid texts. They report improved hybrid-text detection and stronger robustness and generalization outside the training distribution, particularly when few examples are available. The findings suggest that explicitly learning relationships among production processes can help trained detectors handle more varied forms of AI involvement.
neurips-2025-detree-detecting-human-ai-c.tldr: DETree organizes relationships among human–AI writing processes into a hierarchy to improve hybrid-text detection and generalization.

paragraphs: Detecting unfamiliar object classes in a new domain from a few labeled examples requires both accurate localization and strong generalization. The paper identifies complementary strengths: trained detectors locate objects well, while vision foundation models generalize better but are less precise at localization. Its approach combines their features through a mixture-of-experts structure.

An Expert-wise Router chooses relevant foundation-model experts for each detector backbone layer. A Region-wise Router emphasizes foreground information and suppresses background information. Shared and Private Expert Projection modules bring foundation-model features into the detector’s feature space while separating shared and private image features. Together, these components let foundation-model information improve the detector’s internal representations.

The method transfers this generalization capability without changing the detector’s original architecture. It also extends trained detectors to novel classes in unseen domains without retraining on base classes; that is the specific retraining claim supported here. Experiments on multiple cross-domain datasets validate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a structured way to combine existing models’ complementary capabilities for detection with limited target-domain annotations.
neurips-2025-dont-need-retraining-a-mixt.tldr: A mixture-of-experts framework combines detector localization with foundation-model generalization for new domains without retraining on base classes.

paragraphs: Some games have exponentially many possible actions, yet those actions follow an underlying combinatorial structure. Examples include Colonel Blotto and congestion games. This paper studies how players can efficiently learn a coarse correlated equilibrium in such games when their information comes from payoffs, rather than access to full information about the game’s outcomes.

The computational challenge has two parts: both regret and the work required per learning iteration must scale gently with the number of available actions. The authors target growth that is at most polylogarithmic in action-set size. Kernelization had already helped address this challenge with full information, but existing partial-information approaches had impractical or suboptimal runtimes.

The paper introduces a kernelization-based framework for payoff-based learning and applies it to Colonel Blotto, graphic matroid games, and network congestion games. These applications yield computationally efficient learning algorithms with significantly improved runtimes for reaching coarse correlated equilibria compared with prior work. The contribution is to make the games’ structured action spaces useful for efficient learning even under restricted feedback.
neurips-2025-efficient-kernelized-learni.tldr: A kernelization framework improves payoff-based equilibrium learning in several structured games with exponentially large action spaces.

paragraphs: Brain-computer interfaces provide a direct communication route between the brain and external devices, with particular promise for people with severe neurological impairments. Their wider adoption faces obstacles, including low information transfer rates and extensive calibration for each user. Recent work integrating language models has expanded attention from decoding simple commands toward understanding more complex cognitive states.

This position paper argues for extending the field toward Brain-Agent Collaboration. In that framing, an AI agent becomes an active partner in intelligent assistance rather than solely a processor of brain signals. The proposed change concerns how the system’s role is understood: assistance would depend on a collaborative relationship between the person and the agent.

The authors identify ethical data handling, reliable models, and a robust human-agent collaboration framework as central requirements for this direction. They also acknowledge technical hurdles and ethical concerns surrounding agentic deployment. The paper’s contribution is an argument about research priorities and system design, presenting trustworthiness as integral to the proposed extension of brain-computer interfaces.
neurips-2025-embracing-trustworthy-brain.tldr: This position paper proposes Brain-Agent Collaboration as an extension of brain-computer interfaces centered on active assistance and trustworthiness.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit methods must explore possible choices while using the information already available to make rewarding decisions. This paper introduces feature perturbation, which creates exploratory behavior by adding randomness directly to input features. The method moves the source of randomness away from unknown model parameters or observed rewards.

For generalized linear contextual bandits, the authors prove a worst-case regret bound of roughly d times the square root of T, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here, d represents feature dimension and T the number of rounds. This improves the dimension dependence over the roughly d to the three-halves times square root of T bound typical of existing randomized bandit algorithms.

Because the algorithm avoids parameter sampling, the authors describe it as computationally efficient and naturally extendable to nonparametric and neural models. Empirical evaluations report stronger performance than existing methods. The theoretical guarantee is stated for generalized linear bandits, while the broader modeling flexibility concerns the exploration mechanism. Together, these results support perturbing inputs as a simple route to effective exploration with strong regret guarantees.
neurips-2025-exploration-via-feature-per.tldr: Randomizing input features provides efficient bandit exploration with improved dimension dependence in generalized linear regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering produces useful recommendation embeddings, but their numerical coordinates do not directly express concepts a language model can interpret. FACE addresses this mismatch by translating those embeddings into tokens from a pretrained language model. Its goal is to connect recommendation information with the model’s existing semantic capabilities.

The framework first uses a disentangled projection module to split an embedding into concept-specific vectors. A quantized autoencoder then converts continuous representations into discrete tokens, called descriptors. A contrastive alignment objective encourages these descriptors to match the corresponding textual signals. These stages jointly connect the original recommendation representation to language-based meaning.

FACE is model-agnostic and achieves this alignment without fine-tuning the language model itself. Experiments on three real-world recommendation datasets show improvements in benchmark models, while interpretability studies support the meaningfulness of the generated descriptors. The findings suggest that translating collaborative-filtering information into an interpretable token representation can help recommendation systems use pretrained language models more effectively, while also making the translated information easier to inspect.
neurips-2025-face-a-general-framework-fo.tldr: FACE converts collaborative-filtering embeddings into interpretable language-model tokens to improve recommendations without fine-tuning the LLM.

paragraphs: Language models can remain vulnerable to prompts designed to bypass their safety guardrails. Testing these vulnerabilities is difficult when attacks depend on manual tricks or expensive optimization over discrete tokens. The paper introduces GASP, an automated framework for generating readable adversarial prompt suffixes in a fully black-box setting.

GASP uses latent Bayesian optimization to search a continuous representation space associated with a suffix generator. It progressively improves the generator through an iterative refinement procedure that balances attack effectiveness with prompt coherence. The approach targets a central tension in automated testing: prompts need to expose weaknesses while remaining natural enough to avoid the conspicuous wording produced by some optimization methods.

The authors report that GASP produces natural adversarial prompts while significantly improving jailbreak success, reducing training time, and accelerating inference in their experiments. These findings support its proposed use as an efficient, scalable red-teaming framework. The contribution is a way to automate the generation of coherent test attacks without requiring access to the target model’s internal parameters.
neurips-2025-gasp-efficient-black-box-ge.tldr: GASP uses continuous latent-space optimization to generate readable black-box jailbreak suffixes more efficiently for language-model red-teaming.

paragraphs: When a classifier makes a binary decision about someone, that person may change their features to obtain a better outcome. This paper studies how to encourage effort toward features the decision-maker considers desirable. It explicitly accounts for causality: changing one feature can also affect other features, so effort cannot always be understood one coordinate at a time.

The analysis considers the classifier, causal relationships, people’s ability to modify features, and the information they have about the system. With full information, the authors characterize conditions under which people’s choices align with the decision-maker’s goals. They also identify cases where designing a suitable classifier remains computationally tractable despite the problem’s general nonconvexity.

With incomplete information, uncertainty changes the incentives. Agents favor features with high expected impact and low variance, which can often conflict with the decision-maker’s preferred changes. Numerical experiments based on a cardiovascular disease risk study illustrate how desirable modifications can still be encouraged under uncertainty. The work connects classifier design to the causal consequences and perceived reliability of possible actions.
neurips-2025-incentivizing-desirable-eff.tldr: The paper characterizes how causality and uncertainty shape whether strategic classifiers encourage effort toward desirable features.

paragraphs: Generation, representation learning, and classification often rely on separate model designs. Latent Zoning Network explores a shared organizing principle for all three. It creates a Gaussian latent space with disjoint zones, using an encoder and decoder for each data type, such as images or labels.

Tasks become different combinations of those components. A label encoder followed by an image decoder generates a class-conditioned image. An image encoder produces a representation, while an image encoder followed by a label decoder performs classification. This makes the relationship among tasks explicit within the architecture instead of treating each as an unrelated pipeline.

The authors demonstrate three uses. Added to Rectified Flow, LZN improves CIFAR10 FID from 2.76 to 2.59 without changing the training objective. For unsupervised representation learning, it outperforms MoCo and SimCLR on downstream ImageNet linear classification without auxiliary losses. A joint image-and-label version also improves generation FID and achieves state-of-the-art CIFAR10 classification accuracy. These results establish the promise of the shared design across the tested settings.
neurips-2025-latent-zoning-network-a-uni.tldr: Latent Zoning Network combines encoders and decoders in a shared latent space to support generation, representation learning, and classification.

paragraphs: Image watermarking can require recovering a mark from an entire image or from a particular region. MaskWM addresses both through a masking mechanism used during training. Its two variants support different needs: MaskWM-D embeds globally and enables local extraction, while MaskWM-ED embeds and extracts within designated areas.

MaskWM-D follows an encoder, distortion layer, and decoder training design. Before extraction, different masks are applied to watermarked images, teaching the decoder to locate marks and recover them from local areas. MaskWM-ED also supplies the mask to the encoder, directing where the watermark is placed and improving robustness against regional attacks.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance in global and local extraction, localization, and multiple-watermark embedding while maintaining high visual quality. The authors report 20 hours of training on one A6000 GPU and 15-fold computational efficiency relative to WAM. They also describe adjusting the distortion layer to fine-tune robustness requirements. The result is a shared, adaptable framework for both whole-image watermarking and protection of smaller image regions.
neurips-2025-mask-image-watermarking-ffc.tldr: MaskWM uses training-time masks to enable efficient global and regional image watermarking, localization, and extraction.

paragraphs: How narrow can a deep neural network be while still approximating continuous functions? This paper studies that question under the uniform norm, where approximation must control the largest error across the domain. The authors target a substantial gap between known lower and upper bounds on the width needed for universal approximation.

Their framework translates the network question into a geometric function, w(dx, dy), depending only on input and output dimensions. A key step shows that deep, narrow multilayer perceptrons with a small amount of additional width can approximate any twice-continuously-differentiable diffeomorphism. This connects the expressive power of networks to smooth, invertible geometric transformations.

Using that connection, the authors identify the geometric function with the optimal minimum width and apply the Whitney embedding theorem to derive an upper bound: max(2dx + 1, dy) + alpha(sigma). The activation-dependent term lies between zero and two. They also establish new exact values in several settings, including w(2,2) = w(2,3) = 4. The contribution provides both a geometric route to width analysis and concrete sharper results.
neurips-2025-minimum-width-for-deep-narr.tldr: A geometric framework yields new upper bounds and exact minimum widths for universal approximation by deep, narrow neural networks.

paragraphs: An impressive example of a multimodal language model’s output does not reveal how consistently it performs across different abilities. MME addresses that evaluation problem with a benchmark covering perception and cognition across 14 subtasks. Its purpose is to replace reliance on isolated demonstrations with a broader, quantitative assessment.

The instruction-answer annotations are manually designed to address the risk of data leakage from directly reusing public evaluation datasets. Instructions are also deliberately concise. This design is intended to make model comparisons less dependent on elaborate prompt engineering and to make quantitative scoring straightforward. The evaluation format therefore matters alongside the range of abilities being tested.

The authors evaluate 30 advanced multimodal language models using MME. Their findings show substantial room for improvement and identify potential directions for model optimization. The contribution is both a benchmark and a comparative assessment: it supplies a common evaluation structure and uses that structure to expose differences in model capabilities that individual showcase examples may not adequately represent.
neurips-2025-mme-a-comprehensive-evaluat.tldr: MME evaluates 30 multimodal language models across 14 perception and cognition subtasks using manually designed, concise instruction-answer pairs.

paragraphs: Understanding a sound includes understanding where it comes from. Yet many multimodal datasets provide only single-channel audio, limiting research on spatial sound understanding and generation. MRSAudio addresses this gap with recorded spatial audio linked to visual information, motion, and detailed annotations across a range of real-world scenarios.

The dataset has four components covering everyday life, speech, music, and singing. It synchronizes binaural and ambisonic audio with both external-view and first-person video, as well as motion trajectories. Its fine-grained annotations include transcripts, phoneme boundaries, lyrics, musical scores, and prompts. This combination connects sound content with spatial and visual context.

The authors establish five foundational tasks: audio spatialization, spatial text-to-speech, spatial singing synthesis, spatial music generation, and sound-event localization and detection. Their results show that the dataset supports high-quality spatial modeling across these uses. The contribution is a coordinated resource for studying both where sounds occur and how to generate spatial audio, extending the research possibilities beyond those offered by monaural recordings.
neurips-2025-mrsaudio-a-large-scale-mult.tldr: MRSAudio combines spatial recordings, synchronized video, motion trajectories, and detailed annotations to support spatial audio understanding and generation.

paragraphs: Estimating a population mean can require expensive labels even when auxiliary information is readily available. PartiBandits uses that information to decide which labels to request for a variable with k possible classes. Its objective is accurate mean estimation under a limited labeling budget, rather than simply learning the best predictor.

The algorithm has two stages. First, it partitions unlabeled data into groups to reduce average within-group conditional variance. Second, a subroutine called WarmStart-UCB requests labels from those groups round by round. This combines partition learning with adaptive sampling, connecting disagreement-based active learning and upper-confidence-bound methods that were developed for different tasks.

The squared-error bound is, up to logarithmic factors, a sum of the Bayes-optimal classification risk and a rapidly decreasing exponential term, divided by the label count. Consequently, the near-exponential contribution does not remove the dependence on irreducible classification risk. Both stages achieve minimax-optimal convergence rates in classical settings. The authors illustrate the method with simulations using nationwide electronic health records and provide an R implementation.
neurips-2025-near-exponential-savings-fo.tldr: PartiBandits combines learned partitions with adaptive label allocation to estimate population means efficiently, with error depending on Bayes classification risk.

paragraphs: Image-text contrastive learning typically treats a paired image and caption as descriptions of the same concept. Real pairs can disagree, creating a debate over whether to remove that mismatch or make use of it. This paper develops a theoretical account that explains why the answer depends on which semantic information survives the mismatch.

Using latent-variable models, the authors distinguish two mechanisms. Selection bias leaves some semantic variables out of the text. Perturbation bias changes semantic variables between modalities. Under mild assumptions, their analysis shows that learned representations capture exactly the information associated with the semantic variables that remain invariant to both mechanisms.

This result reconciles the competing views by linking misalignment to the information the representation retains. Whether that retained information is useful matters for system design, so misalignment should not be treated as having a single uniform effect. The authors derive practical design insights and validate the theory through extensive studies on synthetic and real image-text data. The empirical results support a nuanced relationship between paired-data mismatch and learned representations.
neurips-2025-on-the-value-of-cross-modal.tldr: Under the paper’s assumptions, multimodal contrastive learning retains semantic information invariant to omissions and alterations across paired modalities.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large pretrained networks consumes substantial memory and computation, motivating methods that update only some parameters. This paper examines how parameter values relate to their gradients. The authors observe that large gradients often occur at small-magnitude weights, and that this relationship is stronger during fine-tuning than during training from scratch.

Based on that observation, they introduce NanoAdam, which dynamically restricts updates to small-magnitude weights. Selecting this subset does not require computing gradients: the selection criterion uses weight magnitudes. The gradient-free claim therefore concerns choosing parameters, rather than claiming that the entire fine-tuning process operates without gradients.

Leaving large-magnitude weights unchanged is intended to preserve features learned during pretraining, since those weights are likely to encode important information. The authors argue that this reduces the risk of catastrophic forgetting. They also report that the method permits larger learning rates and consistently improves generalization in experiments spanning language and vision tasks. The contribution is a simple parameter-selection principle grounded in an observed relationship between weight size and fine-tuning gradients.
neurips-2025-pay-attention-to-small-weig.tldr: NanoAdam dynamically fine-tunes small-magnitude weights, using a gradient-free selection rule motivated by their association with large gradients.

paragraphs: A prediction can change the outcome it is trying to predict when people or institutions act on it. This feedback, called performativity, challenges calibration methods that assume a fixed data-generating distribution. The paper introduces Performative Risk Control to provide statistically grounded calibration in settings where deployment itself influences outcomes.

The framework uses an iteratively refined calibration process. The authors establish theoretical guarantees that predictions improve while remaining risk-controlled throughout that process. They also investigate different risk measures and tail bounds, examining how the statistical choices used to express and bound risk fit into the performative setting.

Numerical experiments on credit-default prediction demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness. The main contribution is to bring explicit risk control into a feedback-sensitive deployment setting, extending the usual focus on static distributions. The authors also position the framework as a safeguard against strategic manipulation in decision-making. That motivation follows from treating responses to model-driven decisions as part of calibration, rather than assuming deployment leaves the environment unchanged.
neurips-2025-performative-risk-control-c.tldr: Performative Risk Control iteratively calibrates models with theoretical risk guarantees when prediction-supported decisions influence subsequent outcomes.

paragraphs: Removing unwanted concepts from text-to-image models can also damage their ability to generate other content. Semantic Surgery addresses this tradeoff through a training-free framework that intervenes in text embeddings before diffusion begins. It adapts the intervention to the concepts detected in each prompt and their estimated strength.

The method estimates target-concept presence and performs a calibrated, scaled vector subtraction to reduce that concept’s influence. A Co-Occurrence Encoding module handles multiple concepts, while a visual feedback loop addresses concepts that persist during denoising. The intervention therefore combines an initial semantic adjustment with continued feedback during generation, without retraining the model.

Experiments cover objects, explicit content, artistic styles, and multiple celebrities. The authors report stronger erasure completeness and robustness than state-of-the-art approaches while preserving unrelated generation and overall image quality. For example, they report a 93.58 H-score for object erasure. They also propose monitoring concept-presence scores as a built-in threat-detection signal. The findings support prompt-sensitive erasure that seeks to remove targeted content while retaining the model’s broader generative abilities.
neurips-2025-semantic-surgery-zero-shot-.tldr: Semantic Surgery dynamically edits text embeddings and uses visual feedback to erase concepts without retraining a diffusion model.

paragraphs: Visual information is not distributed evenly across an image, but many generators represent every image through a dense grid of pixels or latent features. This paper explores a sparse alternative in which a small collection of latent representations carries both image content and information about the regions associated with that content.

The authors first design a sparse autoencoder that reconstructs images with high quality using a small number of latents and their regions of interest, or RoIs. They then train flow-matching transformers jointly on the latent values and RoI values. Generation thus models both the visual representation and its spatial properties without relying on a fixed latent grid.

Experiments show competitive performance relative to dense-grid counterparts with substantially lower computation. On class-conditioned ImageNet generation at 256-by-256 resolution, the method reaches an FID of 2.76 using only 64 latents. The finding supports sparse, spatially located representations as a practical approach to image synthesis, with competitive quality in the evaluated setting despite using far fewer latent elements.
neurips-2025-sparse-image-synthesis-via-.tldr: Jointly generating sparse image latents and their regions of interest delivers competitive image quality with reduced computation.

paragraphs: An approval rule can affect which evidence is submitted for approval. This paper studies that feedback through a principal-agent model: an agent privately assesses a product’s effectiveness and submits data, while a principal chooses a p-value threshold for approval. The agent seeks expected profit, and the principal balances false positives against false negatives.

The game-theoretic model captures how the agent’s participation and reporting respond to the statistical rule. This makes threshold selection a strategic problem because changing the rule can change the evidence-generating interaction. The authors show that the principal’s errors follow clear monotonic patterns when divided into regions by an efficiently computable critical p-value threshold.

That structure yields an interpretable characterization of the principal’s optimal threshold despite the complexity of the interaction. The authors empirically validate the model and its insights using public drug-approval data. The contribution connects statistical testing with the incentives of those supplying evidence, offering a way to analyze approval standards while accounting for how interested parties respond to them.
neurips-2025-strategic-hypothesis-testin.tldr: A game-theoretic model characterizes optimal testing thresholds when approval rules influence strategic participation and evidence reporting.

paragraphs: Adapting a classifier to a new domain without the original training samples makes transferring its decision structure difficult. Discriminative Vicinity Diffusion addresses a variant where the source provider can share both a pretrained classifier and an auxiliary latent diffusion module. That module is trained once on source data without exposing raw source samples during adaptation.

During source training, DVD fits a Gaussian prior over each feature’s nearest neighbors and trains diffusion to move noisy samples toward label-consistent representations. During adaptation, it samples around target features and passes those samples through the frozen diffusion module. An InfoNCE objective aligns the target encoder with the resulting source-like cues, explicitly transferring information about decision boundaries.

DVD outperforms state-of-the-art methods across standard source-free adaptation benchmarks. The same diffusion module also improves source-domain classifier accuracy and performance in supervised classification and domain generalization experiments. The contribution extends latent diffusion beyond generation, using it to convey discriminative knowledge through a shareable module. Its adaptation setting specifically permits that additional module alongside the classifier.
neurips-2025-vicinity-guided-discriminat.tldr: DVD uses a shared, frozen latent diffusion module to transfer source decision-boundary information without accessing raw source samples.

paragraphs: Data valuation seeks to quantify how training data contributes to a model’s outputs, potentially helping address the lack of credit given to data providers. Applying such methods to large language models is difficult because of their computational and memory costs. This paper focuses on making influence functions, a gradient-based valuation method, practical at larger scales.

The authors introduce LoGra, an efficient gradient projection strategy that exploits the structure of gradients during backpropagation. They also provide a theoretical motivation for using gradient projections in influence-function calculations. A companion software package, LogIX, reduces implementation work by allowing existing training code to be converted into data-valuation code with minimal changes.

In experiments using Llama3-8B-Instruct and a one-billion-token dataset, LoGra achieves competitive accuracy relative to more expensive baselines. The authors report up to a 6,500-fold throughput improvement and a fivefold reduction in GPU memory use. These results show that projection can substantially reduce the resource burden of the evaluated attribution workflow while retaining competitive valuation accuracy.
neurips-2025-what-is-your-data-worth-to-.tldr: LoGra makes influence-function data valuation substantially faster and less memory-intensive through structured gradient projection, supported by the LogIX package.
